claims.text: Controlled aging can form nanoscale secondary-phase precipitates in the matrix of a high-entropy alloy.
Nanoscale precipitates produced by aging improve the mechanical durability of the alloy relative to an untreated baseline.
Nanoscale precipitates produced by aging improve room-temperature creep resistance relative to an untreated baseline.
Nanoscale precipitates produced by aging improve corrosion resistance relative to an untreated baseline.
The proposed initial alloy has an as-cast or solution-treated, predominantly single-phase microstructure.
The precipitates act as obstacles to dislocation motion.
Obstructing dislocation motion increases mechanical strength.
Obstructing dislocation motion reduces time-dependent creep deformation at room temperature.
The nanoscale precipitates stabilize grain boundaries.
Precipitation reduces active sites for corrosive attack.
Reducing active corrosion sites improves corrosion resistance.
The aged alloy will have higher yield strength than the untreated alloy.
The aged alloy will have a lower room-temperature creep deformation rate than the untreated alloy.
The aged alloy will have lower corrosion-pit density than the untreated alloy in accelerated corrosion testing.
The untreated alloy lacks the proposed beneficial precipitate microstructure.
The proposed benefit is primarily expected in high-entropy alloy compositions capable of forming useful precipitates under aging conditions.
Compositions that do not form a coherent precipitate phase may not show the proposed property improvements.
